sm: The speaker, Michael Foster, opens at a conference with a joke-filled introduction, then reads Acts 15, verses 36 through 41, about Paul and Barnabas splitting over whether to take John Mark along, and prays. He tells how comedian Norm McDonald was fired from Saturday Night Live over O.J. Simpson jokes and later returned, saying the show had gotten worse rather than him funnier. He applies that to himself: he left the Christian Reformed Church over a dispute about paedocommunion, and he says he is back as a friend because they share the core doctrines of the faith. He announces six principles from Acts 15, the first being that conflict is a normal and necessary part of the Christian life, as seen in the circumcision dispute that led to the Jerusalem Council.

Foster says being a Christian means conflict with the flesh, the kingdom of darkness, and sometimes fellow believers, though servants of God must not be quarrelsome over stupid disputes. He distinguishes peace from mere quiet, saying biblical peace is wholeness and that confronting a problem reveals conflict rather than causes it, as when a church is calmer after removing a contentious member. His second principle is that some conflicts are too sharp for quick resolution and need outside counsel. He says ordinary mutual correction among believers is the first step of church discipline and keeps small things from becoming explosions, while hard disputes justify connectional church government and synods, as Calvin saw in Acts 15. He lists the rules for fighting, namely Matthew 18 for personal offense, Titus 3 for a divisive man, and Proverbs 19:11 for overlooking an offense, which means truly letting it go.

Foster recalls a harsh dispute with a pastor friend that was handled privately with the elders because they would not harm the church over their differences. He says private offenses now become public campaigns while public errors are treated as private, and he suggests sitting on social media posts for a night and asking whether a matter should be overlooked, handled privately, or made public. He says we should act because of who God is, not just to win, and he would attend a hearing on sham charges to speak the truth. His third principle is that intense conflicts are often fueled by family, friendship, social, political, and financial factors. Mark was a relative of Barnabas, but Luke does not say that was Barnabas's motive. He quotes Matthew Henry and Calvin on guarding against partiality and looking only at the cause itself.

Foster notes that in Galatians 2 Peter and even Barnabas withdrew from Gentiles out of fear of the circumcision party, showing that social pressure changes behavior while the theology stays the same. He says an elder may need to recuse himself when family is involved, and that conflicts often have hidden causes like wives, money, fear, or a pastor's reputation. Going off his notes, he warns against jumping from one popular movement or personality to another, saying he wants to be a brother and pastor, not a hero, and that fanboys turn into haters. His fourth principle is that many conflicts come from good things that are not rightly ordered. Paul looked at the mission and would not put Mark back in the role he had abandoned, while Barnabas wanted to give him another chance, and Peter's well-meant rebuke of Jesus in Matthew 16 shows a good affection out of order.

Foster cites Matthew 10:37 and the Larger Catechism to say every duty is not to be done at all times, and that forgiveness does not automatically mean restoration to every responsibility. Paul later asked for Mark as useful to him, which he calls restoration, so he urges the church to say no with love. He tells of his church-planting assessment, of telling people not to plant churches, and of going at night to a drunk friend lying on his kitchen floor to say that love sometimes comforts and sometimes confronts. His fifth principle is that many conflicts have messy resolutions and some things must wait until heaven. The Jerusalem Council settled the gospel but asked for practical accommodations, so one can stand firm on principle while yielding in practice. The part ends as he begins to discuss who was right between Paul and Barnabas.

Foster says Luke does not give a full accounting of fault, and Calvin allowed that both men may have gone too far, so one can be right about a decision and still have something to repent of. Faithful resolution may include concessions, and he gives the example of arguments with his wife Emily that end with mutual repentance and going to bed. He says he did not answer every accusation about leaving his denomination, because protesting too much looks guilty and some things wait for God's judgment, citing First Corinthians 4:5. He has reconciled somewhat with the pastor he fought, and he says he never takes a pound of flesh when an ounce will do. His sixth principle is that not every conflict deserves your attention, citing Proverbs 26:17 about grabbing a passing dog by the ears, and he jokes that he no longer cares about many online disputes.

Foster observes that Paul wanted to visit the brethren he was responsible for, and says Christians should start with the people God has given them. The internet makes distant disputes feel close and lets people feel courageous while avoiding hard conversations with a wife, children, or someone in their own church. He compares this to street preaching being easier than speaking to people you live with, and cites First Thessalonians 4:11 about living quietly. He says he had planned something more controversial but sensed people were tired and hurt from conflict and broken partnerships, and that the movement is now in a grinding, post-pandemic season with some discouragement. He closes by urging the men to pursue peace without relishing controversy, to stand and fight where they must, to put truth and Christ's cause over personal preference, and he ends with a prayer.
